name: Ithmid kohl

card.summary: Ithmid kohl is the traditional antimony-based black eye powder of the Middle East, applied along the lash line to darken and define the eyes.
card.note: Some kohl products are contaminated with lead; the US FDA does not approve kohl as a color additive.

quick.overview:
Ithmid is the Arabic name for the antimony-based kohl powder used for centuries across the Middle East and North Africa. Applied on the inner lid and lash line with a thin stick, it darkens and outlines the eyes, making them look larger and more defined.

It is also used traditionally for eye care and, in Islamic tradition, is mentioned as a recommended practice. Modern research on it is mostly laboratory: a 2024 rabbit study tested ithmid combined with zinc oxide nanoparticles against bacterial eye infection. No human cosmetic trials were identified.
quick.how: The mineral is ground to a fine powder and applied with an applicator stick along the lash line or inner rim of the eyelid, often at night. Many people use it as eyeliner, and it is sometimes combined with other ingredients. Results are immediate.
quick.risks: Kohl products in general have been found to contain high lead levels in some cases, and lead exposure is linked to anemia and developmental problems in children. The US FDA does not list kohl as an approved color additive and considers it unsafe, so importing or selling it in the US is restricted. Eye irritation and contamination are further concerns.

lead: Ithmid is the Arabic term for kohl made from antimony compounds, a fine dark powder applied to the eyelids to darken and outline the eyes [1][2]. Kohl in the broader sense has been used since about 3100 BCE in Egypt, where it was worn across social classes [2].

As a cosmetic it works like a traditional eyeliner: it defines the lash line, makes the eyes look more elongated and emphasizes eye movement, which is why dancers wear it [2]. It also carries protective and medicinal meanings, and ancient Egyptian texts such as the Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BCE) describe kohl as protective for the eyes [2].

Contemporary research includes a 2024 study that tested ithmid kohl with zinc oxide nanoparticles in an induced bacterial eye infection model in rabbits [1]. Regulators and public health researchers have focused on lead contamination in some kohl products [2].

angle.text: Ithmid works as eyeliner: the dark powder defines the lash line and rim, visually enlarging and elongating the eyes. It is one of the oldest forms of eye makeup, still used for everyday and festive looks.

paras: Kohl is traditionally made by grinding stibnite (antimony sulfide); some preparations contain galena (lead sulfide), charcoal or other pigments [2]. Ithmid refers to the antimony form used in Arabic-speaking regions.

Egyptian use dates to around 3100 BCE, and lead isotope analysis suggests Nubians also used and possibly produced kohl between about 2300 and 1500 BCE [2]. In the Horn of Africa, Sahel and South Asia (where it is called surma or kajal), kohl has been worn for beauty, ritual and protection, including at weddings and festivals [2]. In Yemen mothers applied it to infants for protection against the evil eye [2].

No human clinical studies of ithmid as a cosmetic were identified. In a 2024 laboratory and rabbit study, researchers contaminated rabbit eyes with Klebsiella pneumoniae and compared several preparations; the ithmid kohl and zinc oxide nanoparticle ointment was reported as the most effective formulation within two days, and in vitro antibacterial activity was also measured [1]. This is animal research on an infection model, not on cosmetic use.

Early 1990s studies found high lead levels, in some cases up to 84 percent, in certain commercial kohl preparations, and lead-contaminated kohl has been linked to higher blood lead levels, though not all studies agree [2]. A 2016 Pakistani study found lead-containing surma released fine inhalable particles [2]. The US FDA does not list kohl as an approved color additive and states it is unsafe because of possible lead, making its import and sale illegal in the US [2].
